items.question: What kind of research space did you want Cohere for AI to be?
items.object: Cohere for AI’s hybrid research model
items.answer:
About a year and a half ago, Nick and Aidan first approached me with this idea that they wanted to have a research lab. I remember at the time I said to them that they're frankly crazy; that's a lot of work to put together these research labs. But we were thinking about what would be ambitious and what would contribute a different type of research. In my mind, I'd always wanted to do more hybrid research: have a kind of traditional industry lab, but also have these open science initiatives.

Cohere for AI was really, when I joined Cohere a year and a half ago, about creating a new type of research space: working at the frontier of language models and scaling a lot of this infrastructure and engineering, but also creating these cross-institutional ties. We're one of the few spaces where you have both the traditional industry lab, like a Google DeepMind or Microsoft Research, and an open science initiative where we collaborate broadly with researchers all over the world.

items.question: How do you see Cohere for AI’s relationship to the decentralized For AI research lab that preceded Cohere?
items.object: Cohere for AI’s roots in the decentralized For AI research lab
items.answer:
Before Cohere, Ivan and Aidan, two of the founders, had met at the University of Toronto. They actually started something which was a decentralized research lab, very much in the spirit of recreating the spaces in which research exists. They called it For AI. When Aidan and Nick approached me, this was one of the things that swayed me because I knew they already really believed in it; it's where they had both met and connected about research.

Ivan and Aidan published one of the most celebrated research papers that year in Europe out of this For AI decentralized collaborative effort. At the time, Ivan had actually dropped out of school completely, but he was doing research with Aidan, and that's how they started thinking about Cohere. Then Nick joined as a third co-founder. Nick was at Google Brain at the time. For AI really was the foundation of Cohere, and now For AI is a much more ambitious form of the original For AI while still preserving the legacy: this commitment to having new spaces where we can cross-collaborate.

items.question: What is your thinking behind building Cohere for AI around globally distributed talent and open collaboration?
items.object: Cohere for AI's distributed team and open collaboration model
items.answer:
One of my bets was that I wanted to have this open science, this ability to collaborate. I think that's increasingly important because we now see the opposite trend with many labs, but I think it's an important setting, especially for cross-institutional initiatives. Our Aya project covers 101 languages. We also have full-time research staff. My team is distributed: I wanted to take a bet on ML talent, so I have research scientists in Germany, Amsterdam, Canada, the US, Brazil, and Nigeria. We have our research scholars, crafted as entry points into machine learning research, and that's remote-first.

That bet, even with the full-time staff, was that we could find ML talent in many different places in the world. It was a strategic bet as well. When I left Brain, the goal wasn't to reproduce Google Brain, because that wouldn't have been a very productive avenue. We're never going to have 900 people on the research team. My goal is: how do we produce research that's truly different? What are we contributing that's unique? One bet was how we hire: we're hiring talent all over the world. When your talent pool is so big, you find really brilliant people. I'm proud of our full-time research staff; they've produced some incredible work this year.

The other bet was that we should collaborate widely. In contrast to what other labs are doing, where they're increasingly locking down, we should lean into openly collaborating. A perfect example is the Aya project, which involves independent researchers all over the world, from traditional academic institutions like MIT and from people just starting their journey. The two bets are well balanced, but they're both part of the bet that we should be producing a different type of research, and that as a lab we're only going to produce something meaningful if we're also changing the spaces in which research is done.

items.question: How do you see the Aya project's opportunity to bring generative AI breakthroughs to languages beyond English?
items.object: The Aya project's approach to multilingual generative AI
items.answer:
Aya is truly something I would describe as perseverance. It's an effort to bring together researchers all over the world and make these models not just English-first.

In some ways, we've had this exciting set of breakthroughs where we now have incredible capability for generative AI in English. A few ingredients went into those breakthroughs. One is scale. The other is this structured data, instruction fine-tuning, where you have questions and answers. Structuring the data in that way has led to a big leap in zero-shot performance and the ability of these models to perform well on unseen tasks. The third thing is preference training. Having preferences about what we prefer really helps tune these models.

The scale benefits both English and multilingual, but the fact that we have no data outside English for a lot of this instruction fine-tuning is what holds back these leaps in technology for other languages. It's also timely because one thing we get when we scale is that we require less data to see these gains in performance. We can get away with smaller amounts of data. It's the perfect time to think about how to make this coverage exist for other languages, because we don't need much; we just need to focus on high-quality contributions.

That's the Aya project: a bet that if we work with researchers all over the world and focus on optimization techniques that work well for other languages, we're going to see these breakthroughs. We're covering 101 languages, so it's going to be the biggest open-source model released for languages all over the world, and it will be released next January. It is a generative model, but we're also doing multilingual red teaming. Even safety is typically only done in English, so we're doing red teaming across multiple languages as well.

items.question: How do you see Aya’s work on multilingual models as complementary to BLOOM?
items.object: Aya’s relationship to BLOOM
items.answer: I think BLOOM is really special. It focused on pretraining, which is also really important. We almost have multiple stages. We have these pretrained models on the internet, and even when we crawl the internet, choices have been made that mean English is overrepresented. BLOOM was an effort to restructure that pretraining data so you have better coverage. Their goal was 47 languages. I would describe our effort as complementary. items.question: How do you see existing multilingual instruction data falling short of what people value in today's language models?
items.object: Multilingual instruction data and traditional NLP benchmarks
items.answer:
There's a really interesting data quality challenge. A lot of data is poor quality, especially when you get outside of English. One thing we noticed early on is that this is a wider crisis the whole field is facing. All our traditional academic benchmarks are around these very discrete, one-word answers. We measure performance based on the ability to correctly classify the sentiment of something. That's because for a lot of natural language processing, we spent decades crafting very narrow, task-specific measurements of success. Now we have these universal models, and what we appear to like most are fluid responses, longer completions. This is what feels most exciting and interesting about these models: they're able to engage in a way that feels very fluid.

Moving toward that requires an entirely different type of data. A lot of the existing instruction-style data for multilingual falls flat; it leads to too short a completion. You'll see this if you look at existing open-source models for multilingual: they'll generate very short completions. Our goal is to get longer completions and weight the type of data correctly.

items.question: Which optimization challenges do you want the Aya project to tackle in its next stage?
items.object: The Aya project's next-stage optimization challenges
items.answer: We've focused on dataset augmentation. The optimization challenges I want us to tackle in the second stage of this project next year are tokenization, which typically does not work at all for scripted languages like Hindi, Arabic, Japanese, and Korean, and preference training. Preference training has been the spark that has really unlocked a lot of potential in English. We tell the model which one we prefer, and that's used to guide model completions through reinforcement learning by human feedback, or something else that's optimization-based. What's the problem if you have 101 languages? Do you need preference data for all 101? items.question: How do you weigh model size against the number of languages covered when choosing a pretrained base for a multilingual model?
items.object: The tradeoff between model capacity and language coverage in multilingual pretraining
items.answer: There's a perhaps more interesting question, though: let's say we take a smaller model. For example, mT5 is another model released by Google; it's open source, so it's a valid base we can play with. mT5 only goes up to 13 billion parameters, but it covers 101 languages. Here's the interesting question: if you scale that, is it more valid to have a 100-billion-plus model trained on fewer languages as a pretrained base, or do you still want a smaller model trained on more? The main bottleneck for representing languages is that you need more capacity to represent them. It's called the curse of multilinguality. The more languages you need, the more you need to scale; otherwise you cannibalize from some languages to represent others. Your question is interesting because one thing we want to explore is a 52B and 100B model for fewer languages in pretraining and see how scaling impacts it. Maybe it's okay to go with fewer languages as long as you scale up, because fine-tuning covers all the languages and you might still get a lot of value there.

items.question: How do you think data quality changes the amount of model capacity needed to train deep neural networks?
items.object: Data quality and model capacity in deep learning
items.answer:
It's really this question of whether we need all of the capacity that we throw at these training regimes. There have been two trends that characterized our field for the last decade: more parameters is better, and more data is better. They've been frustrating trends because they're painfully simple. We're researchers, but we just throw more data or more parameters at the problem.

This is asking why we need so much data, what we get with the data, and whether, if we cared more about data quality, we could get away with less and still perform as well. For me, this is part of a broader inflection point in the field. For a long time it was really hard to get my colleagues to care about data. The premise of how people thought about deep neural networks was that you don't have to care about data because you allow the model to deal with it; you delegate representation to the model. I think now we're at this point where, yes, you can do that, but it's incredibly costly because you pay for it in terms of number of parameters. If your data is junk, you're just regularizing your model; you need a lot more capacity to compensate for the junk data and still extract value.

This was originally part of a series of work I did on what a model forgets when you remove most of the parameters. When you remove 90%, it forgets noisy or rare examples, which tells us that 90% of the weights in the model are used to compensate for these really noisy examples. This data pruning effort is the belief that if you isolate higher-quality data, you can get away with a lot less in training time and capacity.

items.question: What do you find significant about the “Less Is More” paper's approach to data pruning for pretraining?
items.object: The “Less Is More” paper on data pruning for pretraining
items.answer:
The paper was led by Max, and it's work I'm really proud of because it looks at data pruning at scale. When we do pretraining, that's where the cost of training these models is. It's expensive for two reasons: you're processing a lot of data, typically crawling the internet and extracting unsupervised text, and training on it in an unsupervised way; also, the amount of data is so huge you barely get through an epoch. That's why in NLP people often talk about one epoch of training as the standard, which is fascinating. That's why people talk about running out of data: it's based on the assumption that we're only ever going to train on something once, whereas computer vision is the opposite; people train on it for 90 epochs and see the same data point 90 times.

This question is, do we need to train on everything? If we train on less, we can probably see it more times. We show you can get away with a lot less: with 30% you can still achieve equivalent performance, which is remarkable. But it matters how you select for high-quality data. We benchmark three techniques of different computational intensity. Computational efficiency is essential since you're trying to score the internet and determine what's good quality over the entire internet. We find that simple methods for scoring what's good are far better than very expensive methods. It's puzzling why, but even a very cheap signal about what's good can be a viable path for data pruning, so people should use it as a first step.

items.question: How do you interpret the performance of perplexity compared with L2 norm and memorization scores for data pruning?
items.object: Perplexity versus L2 norm and memorization scores for data pruning
items.answer:
We compared three techniques. One was, in many ways, the simplest: perplexity. Perplexity is generated every time somebody's put through a model, so this is almost the crudest model signal you could possibly have. The second was much more expensive: L2 norm, proposed in a different setting as a pruning metric for understanding what weights are important—not within the data space, within the weight space. It requires computationally expensive calculations. You need to see how the gradient norm changes over various checkpoints, so you have to take snapshots across model training. I believe the suggested one was over 15 model trainings, so you have to have 15 separate models trained independently and then compute how much the gradient norm changes.

The third was memorization score, also quite expensive. Both L2 and memorization score were not proposed for data pruning, so we were trying them in a context they weren't originally imagined for. We compared that with the baseline: does this outperform random selection? A good method should at least be better than randomly choosing what data to keep. We found that only perplexity did so. Perplexity was the only metric that consistently outperformed, which suggests we have a lot more work to do for formally rigorous methods. Clearly, the methods we've proposed that are very rigorous, when tested in this setting, aren't up to par with a very simple model signal.

items.question: How do you think adaptive training could make models more efficient?
items.object: Adaptive training and model efficiency
items.answer:
One reason I'm attracted to data pruning is that we seem to have the least efficient way for training these models right now. We show all the examples to the models the same amount of times, whether that's one or 90 times. No matter how difficult or simple the data point is, it's presented to the model. That's not how humans work. When we find something challenging, we squint in, ask, 'Tell me more,' or ask a clarifying question. We have a high degree of saliency that makes us more efficient because we spend more time on hard things and less time on easy things.

The overall direction I think is fascinating, and data pruning fits in as a simple example: you put zero attention on some examples and 100% on others. The future is adaptive training in general, where over the course of training you adaptively identify what is salient for your learning procedure and spend more capacity there. Right now we allocate the same amount of capacity to all examples. I see this from a few directions. Data pruning is one, but how we use the weights within a model is another. Right now we do global updates, which means no matter what, you're updating all your weights for an incoming batch. This doesn't really make sense. We need more modular capacity, fusing and merging of different model sections. Another work from the lab, led by Ted, was mixture of experts. For me, mixture of experts is one of the first steps in this direction of having more decomposable components and adaptive capacity where you can route. Data pruning and general adaptive capacity are how I think we're going to create more efficient models. Right now we show all the examples, update all weights, and do the same number of forward passes. One of our great benefits in navigating the world and efficiency is that we can choose to ignore and choose how we allocate attention.

items.question: What do you find compelling and challenging about mixture-of-experts models?
items.object: Mixture-of-experts models
items.answer:
It's a beautiful idea. In some ways it gets at the essence of how do we create something where we have specialization instead of just massive models where you update everything. You have a model which might be better at coding than generating or processing French prompts.

One challenge is, frankly, they're very hard to train. They tend to be very sensitive. Because you're doing routing, you have to decide where something goes. Experts can become biased early on in training. If an expert is favored early on, it gets favored repeatedly, which means there are all sorts of tricks to ensure you don't choose your favorite expert early and then end up sending it everything. The crudest trick, which is widely used, is load balancing with random routing. During training you might randomly allocate, but I'm sure we can do better; it's one of the open questions.

The second tricky thing is that when you deploy these models, you have to hold all the different experts in memory, because you need the expert ready if it gets chosen. This is very challenging for making these models usable. One of the works we did, from an operational scalability perspective, was about the amount of memory needed in the machine to hold all these checkpoints of fairly big models and call the one that's needed.

In general, mixture of experts is an exciting direction because it's shown clear breakthroughs on certain tasks.

items.question: Why do you see your lab's Ted-led work on parameter-efficient mixture-of-experts models as an important direction?
items.object: Ted-led research combining mixture of experts with parameter-efficient modules
items.answer: Our work, led by Ted, was about making mixture of experts extremely parameter-efficient, using 1–2% of the weight updates so we only update a few weights. items.question: How do you understand the appeal of mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures compared with training a single massive model?
items.object: The appeal of mixture-of-experts architectures compared with a single massive model
items.answer:
There's no denying that one reason people gravitate toward MoEs is the idea that it reduces the effective number of FLOPs. The bigger you go, typically the more FLOPs you have. These are matrix multiplies, floating-point operations. With MoE, because you don't go deep, you're going massively wide: you have many models to choose from. Your individual models can be big, but they're not extremely big, and instead you're focusing on routing as the magic. You reduce your FLOPs. That's almost certainly a practical constraint, because you can essentially have way more compute, but your latency or necessary compute at serving time is much lower because you're not using all of it.

I think that's still one of the motivating factors behind MoE. Of these two components—effective compute, minimizing FLOPs, and specialization ability—I would say specialization as an observed property is sometimes not immediately clear with these trained models. Sometimes we don't see that one model only does code and another always does French. What's motivating the interest right now is more this effective-compute argument. What motivates the general interest in why this architecture is special is the idea that if we do it better, because optimization is still very unknown with this type of architecture, we can get that specialization. But you're right: if it were feasible to train a massive model instead, there would probably be more exploration in that direction. I don't think it means scaling laws are petering out. I think it's very difficult to train models of that size while still preserving training dynamics.

items.question: How do you assess mixture-of-experts models as a way to achieve specialization?
items.object: Specialization in mixture-of-experts models
items.answer:
Typically they're trained together. You want to learn the routing; the routing is the magic of mixture of experts. But there are a lot of tricks to stabilize your routing. One is that you could have different learning rates for different experts, trying to stabilize it by making sure experts get updated at different rates. It induces the experts to learn different things. The overall goal is typically to take these experts, learn them jointly, and try to induce specialization.

In this case, what's interesting is that we haven't observed much specialization. I don't know about the concrete aspects of GPT-4 because it wasn't published, but we know from other published papers that it's very hard to induce data specialization, especially if you use random shuffling, which tends to work the best. For most models today, random shuffling of data is hard to beat. Even with mixture of experts, the shuffling is preserved the same way as it is for other models: it will be randomly shuffled. We see some differences in the ability of these models to specialize, but it feels a bit cherry-picked.

We explored this in our paper. We looked at the differences between showing the mixture of experts tokens versus embeddings. If you show embeddings, it's much more of a heavy prior on the topic, imposing a heavier onus toward specialization. We found this actually hurt performance; it wasn't as competitive as just showing the tokens. Sometimes efforts to induce specialization result in worse performance. It does seem like the driving factor for why people love these models isn't the inherent goal of why they were first designed. I still think that's partly due to the paucity of what optimization works for this type of model. I'm optimistic we'll see better recipes to induce specialization. As someone who cares a lot about adaptive computation, I still think of mixture of experts as a really interesting direction. People use it widely now more for energy conservation: it's a clever technique to scale across rather than scale deep, and that has resulted in nice performance gains.

items.question: How do you understand the role of hardware in determining which machine learning ideas succeed?
items.object: Hardware's influence on which machine learning ideas succeed
items.answer:
A perfect example is that GPUs unlocked deep neural networks. Think back to 2012 and why convolutional networks were basically adopted overnight: GPUs over the 2000s had been intentionally, slowly repurposed from video games to work with convolutional neural networks. That was the trick; it allowed much deeper networks, which turned out to be the crucial ingredient that was missing. For decades, researchers working on deep neural networks had been marginalized. I think it's one of the most interesting examples of tooling playing an aiding factor in when ideas are recognized.

That paper came from trying to understand some of my own ideas and their incompatibility with hardware. Sparsity is a widely used compression idea in research forums because it achieves the best levels of compression, but it doesn't play well with GPUs. There are no gains because our computer science and hardware field has been built around matrices, with inputs in a structured form. An unstructured form, where some things are sparse and some aren't, results in no gain because it still has to be put into a matrix for the hardware to recognize it.

items.question: What do you see the Grand Illusion paper's findings on JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch portability revealing about hardware lock-in in machine learning?
items.object: The Grand Illusion paper and hardware lock-in in machine learning frameworks
items.answer:
I wanted to ask how locked in we really are. We know we're locked in, but it's hard to tell because we often only realize after the fact what was holding us back. We only realized GPUs were critical for deep neural networks after 2012. How can we tell how bad the situation is?

The paper asks how portable mainstream frameworks—JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch—are. They're purported to be general frameworks, Python libraries, the workhorses of ML, used by millions around the world. Most ideas, probably 99.9%, are developed in one of these frameworks. How portable are they, or how locked in are they to their hardware? These frameworks, even though they report to be general, are extremely locked into underlying hardware. For example, when you try to transfer PyTorch to TPUs, 40% of all functions fail. If you need to translate an idea to different hardware, it's just not usable. We also find massive slowdowns in performance, sometimes untenable. Some functions just fail to transfer across completely in a usable way.

All this means there are first-class citizens for each type of hardware. JAX is a promising software framework because there are hardly any failures; everything works on TPUs and GPUs. But you see massive slowdowns on GPUs: more than 90% of all functions have massive slowdowns, because it's been developed with TPUs in mind.

The big picture is that we don't have a sense of how our field is narrowing. It's happening with software and architectures: everything is basically built on Transformers. You see hardware overfit to Transformers, which means it'll be harder and harder to make the next stepwise shift to a totally different architecture. NVIDIA even called its latest H100 a Transformer accelerator, although that was clever marketing and there wasn't really anything under the hood that wasn't just acceleration.

items.question: Why do you see software portability as crucial to enabling innovation in machine learning?
items.object: Software portability as a way to enable research innovation
items.answer:
I think that's partly why I wanted to focus on software portability. A lot of our research innovation is empirical. No one wanted to acknowledge deep networks before they empirically worked. To get empirical evidence, you have to make the cost of iteration cheaper. You have to make it easier for people to experiment across different settings and understand the limitations and settings in which methods work.

For me, software portability is crucial because the ability to experiment on different hardware is crucial. Some hardware facilitates certain subsets of functions, so even documenting the latency of functions across hardware is part of this wider benchmarking. As we get even narrower in what types of software are supported, we need ways to evaluate which software frameworks are getting better and which are getting worse. This is part of a wider initiative. The crucial thing in enabling innovation is decreasing the cost of switching and increasing the benefits of doing ablations on different types of hardware. That only works if we decrease the cost of it all.

items.question: What does early exiting illustrate for you about the software lottery in machine learning research?
items.object: The software lottery and early exiting
items.answer:
We also point to concrete examples where ideas have not been able to be pursued because of the software lottery. One is early exiting. The main benefit is that you don't have to pass something through the entire network; you can exit early if the example is easy. You gain a lot, but it doesn't work at all with TensorFlow. Why? It initializes the graph at the beginning. This is a graph-style software program, and because the entire network is represented in the graph, you don't gain any memory because you can't modify it once initialized.

There are things like this where we're trying to call out areas where compiler-level developers and hardware experts need to get close in the room and see the tension points. I often find the most important first step in these problems is to characterize the severity of the issue. I'm proud of this work because it does that in a grumpy way, but in a needed way. We need to start collaborating with hardware architects and software architects.

items.question: Why do you see creating a common language between hardware architects and algorithm developers as an important goal of your software portability work?
items.object: A common language between hardware architects and algorithm developers
items.answer:
Part of our goal is to create a common language to bridge these different subfields. One reason this is so unexplored is that hardware architects typically have separate training, siloed jargon, and don't really talk to algorithm developers. Most algorithm developers, like myself, build models and are stuck with the hardware we get; we don't influence the next generation of hardware.

Codesign has become a prevalent concept only recently, and it's still awkward. The timelines are different: the time to produce a new algorithm is much shorter than the timeline to produce a new generation of hardware. Part of what I see these efforts doing is giving us a common language to articulate pain points. I might not know the jargon needed to describe what changes need to happen to a compiler, but I know what functions are most impacted by this lack of portability. If they're central to my idea, I have a language to express why it's important that we support them. That's often the first crucial piece in creating better cohesion between distinct communities that don't talk much because their training and cultures are so siloed.

Hardware architects also have a very different culture. ML researchers tend to favor a primarily open-source community. Even the social sites used are different: hardware architects are always on LinkedIn. I now have several ongoing collaborations with different hardware architects. It's fascinating.

items.question: Why do you think AI chatbots have connected with everyday people more deeply than earlier breakthroughs like convolutional neural networks?
items.object: The public’s emotional connection with AI chatbots
items.answer: I think we're at an interesting time because it's very rare that the ideas you work on are adopted by millions of people overnight. Clearly, some of this technology is connected in a much deeper, very fundamental, emotional way with the general population: people who are not researchers and people who are not developers. That didn't happen with previous breakthroughs like convolutional neural networks. They were widely applied, so they probably live behind your phone in different apps, but they didn't connect with the everyday person in a similar way. This has emotionally connected with people. Most people have played with a chatbot over the last few months; most have experimented and probed it. I think part of it is that it feels very interpretable to people. The ability to probe through chat and see the responses and identify where the model fails and where it's good has connected people to the idea of playing with an algorithm in a much more visceral way than they ever felt with computer vision, which was typically for a few narrow tasks and always behind the hood. People didn't really probe a computer vision model. This means all the emotions that come with people experiencing new technology. From the researcher side, the amount of interest has forced the question: this was a research idea adopted widely overnight; how do we make sure it's used responsibly, and what are the risks? Whenever a tool is powerful, you have amplified risk as well as amplified impact.

items.question: How do you understand the values divide in the AI community between concern about future models and concern about currently deployed models?
items.object: The values divide between addressing future AI risks and risks from currently deployed models
items.answer: The values divide is that there's a sense that this is part of a wider march toward much more performant models, and our focus should be on making sure those are developed in a way that is not a threat to humans and human welfare. This is what I would call the focus on existential risk. For people concerned about current models, this is sometimes in tension with feeling that we need enough resources to make sure our currently deployed models don't amplify risks like misinformation. I'm really concerned that we've created models where generated text is not distinguishable to a human, so we've lowered the barrier to creating information. That's positive in some cases; it enables people to communicate and be creative in new ways. On the negative side, we've lowered the barrier to entry for problematic uses of information creation. Top of my mind is how we invest in directions that could help us identify text generated by a model and have good traceability for models, knowing how they're being used in different places. If I were to characterize the divide between those focused on future models and those focused on current ones, it's more a divide about where resources should be allocated. If you care a lot about existential risk, often you care about use cases like biosecurity threats. For me, this is a compelling risk; it tends to have an immediacy for those who hear about it. If a language model can describe how to build a bomb, that's a visceral risk. But is that the most frequent risk we'll see in how people actually use these models? If that's the risk we care about, I think it's addressable. But does that displace the conversation about other risks? We've created universal models that can be used for many use cases, and certain use cases occupy a lot of discussion and displace other equally important conversations: how do we make sure these are representative, and how do we make sure they cover languages—

items.question: How do you assess the Frontier Model paper's framework as a basis for AI policy?
items.object: The Frontier Model paper's framework for identifying and governing risky AI models
items.answer:
The paper proposed that a frontier model is a model with a likelihood of being able to cause a serious negative impact to human welfare, and to demonstrate, perhaps in the vein of emergent abilities, that certain abilities emerge when you scale that are considered quite harmful.

What I would say, and what I would consider an LLM to be, wouldn't be a frontier model under the terms of this paper. That's where I would push. The paper came out of a workshop, so it was fun to grapple with this with co-authors who all had different ideas of what risk is. But how do you tell? What's the inflection point where an LLM is not a frontier model, but then becomes one? That's where it gets harder. I don't think the paper resolves that. It talks about what should happen when it becomes a frontier model, but the meat of the question—the thing needed to implement this as policy—is how do you identify when it happens, and is it a binary moment? Can a model be a frontier model and then regress and be a non-frontier model?

As soon as you think about the nuances, you realize this is difficult to implement in practice, because we don't have standard ways of evaluating. What do we evaluate for when it's a universal model and we expect it to do everything? Let's say you're highly performant in one skill that might lead to risk; does that mean it's a frontier model? If we only care about one attribute, what is it? Is it biosecurity? If I know I'm going to be evaluated as a frontier model on biosecurity, I'll just make sure my model doesn't produce recommendations for biosecurity. But these models are like that water bottle: when you slosh it to one side to solve one thing, you'll take it away from another. For me, that's the crux of the question.

When you talk about that level of detail, you're back to current risk. If we can't measure current risk appropriately, how are we measuring this transition inflection point to frontier AI? I like conversations like that when we're all in the same room working on a paper. That's the type of grappling we need to make sure perspectives are anchored. I like to focus on the challenges we have with current risk because they compound when you project out.

items.question: How do you view the range of approaches within the AI existential-risk research community?
items.object: The AI existential-risk research community and its approaches
items.answer:
To be honest, it's not that side; it's a side. I know and collaborate with a lot of existential-risk collaborators. In some ways they're my colleagues; we're all researchers, smart people interrogating what these models do and what their capabilities are.

I think there's a variety of perspectives, even within existential risk, mainly because it's so underspecified as a concept. What do you mean by existential risk? What is a risk significant enough to be a threat to human life or existence? What's the timeline? The more underspecified your problem is, the easier it is to have many different approaches and formulations that fit within it. It's the same with machine learning: it's specified in terms of a goal, but there are many approaches. Even this notion of AGI means something dramatically different to different people. It's as much a value concept as it is a technical objective.

That is probably my most grumpy point, and I've said it to my colleagues: when something is very underspecified, it's hard to hold people accountable. I think there are many different approaches to existential risk. When you get down to the technical details, they're often lacking, although there are excellent researchers doing great work in the space and building technical frameworks. One example is red teaming for biohazard risk. I think that was done in a really rigorous and interesting way. There's probably a difference of opinion about whether that's the only type of risk to focus on for red teaming or a case study in how to do red teaming.

The more underspecified your problem is, the easier it is to have many different approaches and formulations that fit within it. It's the same with machine learning: it's specified in terms of a goal, but there are many approaches. Even this notion of AGI means something dramatically different to different people. It's as much a value concept as it is a technical objective.

That is probably my most grumpy point, and I've said it to my colleagues: when something is very underspecified, it's hard to hold people accountable. I think there are many different approaches to existential risk. When you get down to the technical details, they're often lacking, although there are excellent researchers doing great work in the space and building technical frameworks. One example is red teaming for biohazard risk. I think that was done in a really rigorous and interesting way.
